children.text: Two lagoons lie side by side between the limestone cliffs of Coron Island. You cross by ladder at high tide and through a gap under the water at low tide, and as you swim you can feel layers of cool and warm water for yourself.

Twin Lagoon is a pair of small bays tucked into the shore of Coron Island. Inside a ring of steep limestone cliffs, an outer lagoon that opens to the sea and an inner lagoon lie side by side, divided by a single low limestone wall. Seen from above, the two pools look like twins, with a ridge of rock running between deep blue-green water.

The real appeal here is not what you see but what you feel on your skin. Reviews say that as you swim you can feel the water temperature change from one stretch to the next, and one description says the inner lagoon is warmer and a mix of fresh and salt water. Geothermal heat is sometimes given as the reason, but the exact cause is unclear, so it is hard to say for certain. Reviewers describe the sensation differently, so the best way to know is to feel it yourself.

The second feature is that the way across depends on the tide. At high tide you climb over the wall on a wooden ladder, and at low tide you can swim through a gap beneath it. The same place shows a different face several times a day.
Coron Island is the ancestral land of the indigenous Tagbanwa people, and it was officially recognized as their ancestral domain on
June 5, 1998

. The community manages the entrance fee. This is not a place you only look at but one you experience by swimming and reading the tide, so it suits travelers who enjoy being in the water, and because it is on almost every Coron island tour, it is easy to fit into your plans.

Float face down, swim slowly, then let your legs hang down. Many reviewers say the water temperature feels different from one stretch to the next, and some describe the boundary between layers as a hazy shimmer. Once the water gets churned up the feeling fades, so go early when it is calm.

blocks.title: Cross under the wall at low tide

children.text: When the tide is out, you can swim through the gap beneath the limestone wall between the two lagoons. The way is narrow, so you may have to queue when it is busy, and guides sometimes stop it on days with waves or currents. If you are not confident in the water, ask before you try.

blocks.title: Climb over by ladder at high tide

children.text: When the water is high, you go over the wall by a wooden ladder and a short deck to the other side. Wet wood is slippery, so go up and down slowly, and aqua shoes with non-slip soles make it much safer.

blocks.title: Swim beneath the cliffs of the inner lagoon

children.text: In the inner lagoon, tall limestone cliffs come down to the water. Reviewers say it is deeper than expected and there are few places to put your feet down, so look around floating in a life jacket and do not go far.

blocks.title: Paddle a kayak in the outer lagoon

children.text: The outer lagoon is where boats dock, so a kayak suits it better than swimming. There are reportedly no rental stands on site, so it is safer to arrange a kayak when you book the tour, and prices differ by operator, so confirm when you book. Some visitors say the swim across is enough on its own.

blocks.title: See the wooden walkways under the cliff

children.text: In the rock face there are walkways and small piers held up by wooden posts. It is a spot where you can take in the water color, the grain of the limestone and the shallow bottom below at a glance, and a waterproof camera works well here.

blocks.title: Combine it with other Coron island tour stops

children.text: Twin Lagoon is usually bundled in one day with places like Kayangan Lake, CYC Beach and the Skeleton Wreck. Your arrival time depends on which stop comes first, so ask the order when you book.

items.title: Early-morning half-day route
items.subtitle: For feeling the thermocline in peace

children.text: Board a private boat or an early-departing tour at the Coron town pier. The night before, check the tide table and ask them to time the visit for low tide.
After a boat ride of about
30 minutes–1 hour
you reach Twin Lagoon. Pay the entrance fee of about
and put on a life jacket.
At this quiet hour, loosen up in the first lagoon and then cross to the inner lagoon.
In the inner lagoon, put your face in the water and swim slowly to feel the thermocline. About
30–40 minutes
at a time is plenty.
Leave before the group boats arrive and head to your next stop.
The order of stops differs by tour company, so you may not be able to visit Twin Lagoon first. Be sure to check the order when you book.
You are picked up at your accommodation and taken to the pier.
The Coron island tour boat departs. It often stops at Kayangan Lake first.
You arrive at Twin Lagoon. It can be crowded at this hour, so if the line is long, swimming in the inner lagoon first and crossing later also works.
Lunch on the boat at an island beach.
Snorkel at the Skeleton Wreck or a coral garden.
Return to the Coron town pier.

items.title: Tide-timed private route
items.subtitle: For passing under the wall at low tide

children.text: The day before, check the Coron tide table and pick the time of the lowest tide. For the latest tides, check a weather and marine forecast yourself.
Ask the captain and guide to plan the route so you reach Twin Lagoon at that time. Unless you have a private boat, it is hard to change the order.
Arrive about an hour before low tide, warm up in the first lagoon, and cross under the wall when the water is lowest.
On the way back the water begins to rise, so you can use the ladder instead. If there are waves or currents, follow the guide's judgment.
Direct flights from Manila to Coron ended on
March 29, 2026

. Philippine Airlines and Cebgo stopped turboprop flights at Ninoy Aquino Airport and moved the Busuanga (Coron) route to Clark International Airport. From Manila, you now have to travel to Clark and fly from there.
A P2P bus from Manila to Clark Airport takes about

The fast ferry from El Nido takes about

From Manila, 2GO large ferries run about twice a week, take

children.text: From Busuanga Airport to Coron town by van takes about
30 minutes
at a flat rate of about

items.title: From Coron town to Twin Lagoon

children.text: You cannot reach Twin Lagoon by land, only by boat. It is included in Coron island tours that leave from the Coron town pier, or you can rent an outrigger boat, and the trip takes about
30 minutes–1 hour
depending on the route.

Join tours usually pick you up at your accommodation in the morning and finish late in the afternoon. A private boat lets you choose the departure time and order, which makes it good for matching the tide.
In northern Palawan, where Coron is, the dry season runs from
December
to
May
and the rainy season from
June
to
November
. In the dry season the sea is calm and visibility is good, so the lagoon colors are at their clearest.

The thermocline is easier to feel when the water is calm. On days of heavy rain or rough waves the layers can mix and the boundary blur, so it pays to choose the calm early morning. If a typhoon approaches, island tours stop altogether, so leave some slack in your schedule.

The tide changes every day regardless of the season. If you want to cross under the wall at low tide, look up that day's tide first and talk with your guide about whether the way across suits that time.

items.note: Per night in a hostel, mid-range costs more

children.text: Prices are rough estimates as of
and may vary with local conditions.
There are no accommodations or restaurants around Twin Lagoon, so staying in Coron town and going out by boat is in effect the only way. Hostels and guesthouses (about
per night) are clustered in the town center near the pier, which makes early-morning departures easy. Mid-range hotels cost more, and a sea-view resort means a longer trip.

Tour lunch is commonly fish and pork that the boat crew bought at the local market, grilled over charcoal and served with rice and fruit. There may be no shop at Twin Lagoon, so bring water and snacks on the boat. Coron town has several seafood restaurants that will grill a fish you pick from the market on the spot, which makes them a good place for dinner after the tour.
To enjoy it quietly, choose a route that arrives early, right after opening. It tends to be crowded in the daytime when tour groups gather, so going early gives you more space.
The entrance fee is about
and is often included in the tour price. Check whether it is included when you book, and bring a little cash.
Wearing a life jacket is the rule at the lakes around Coron. Following the instructions on site is safer.
Check the tide the day before and ask for Twin Lagoon to fall at low tide. Join tours rarely change the order, so a private boat has the advantage.
To feel the thermocline, let your legs hang down in your life jacket. The water at your toes may feel different in temperature from layer to layer.
There are reportedly no kayak rentals on site, so it is safer to reserve in advance. Prices differ by operator, so confirm the exact amount when you book.
Bring aqua shoes, a dry bag and sunscreen. The ladder and rocks are slippery when wet.
A waterproof camera or case is good for capturing the boundary in the water and its color.

Reviews describe Twin Lagoon as deep, with few places to put your feet down. Non-swimmers and children must wear a life jacket, and no one should go far out in the inner lagoon. Entry rules and fees can change by community decision, so check the latest notice before you visit.
Passing through the gap under the wall at low tide is recommended only for strong swimmers. On days with waves or currents, follow the guide's instructions and use the ladder or do not cross.
The ladder and decks are very slippery when wet. Go up and down slowly one person at a time and hold the rope that serves as a handrail.
Limestone is sharp and corals live here. Do not grab or step on rocks, and use reef-safe sunscreen.
This is the ancestral domain of the Tagbanwa people. Leave no trash, follow your guide, and ask permission before photographing people.
On days with typhoons or monsoon winds, tours are canceled or timings change. It is safest not to schedule a tour the day before your flight home.
The lake most often visited on the same Coron island tour. You climb the viewpoint stairs and swim in a brackish lake, and its water has a different character from Twin Lagoon.
The starting point of the tours and the base where accommodations and restaurants are. You can combine the Mount Tapyas sunset and a hot spring into one day.
An island south of Coron, a historic town that had a leprosarium in the early 20th century. It makes a good one-day trip for a quiet town and the sea.
A resort area of limestone lagoons about
3 hours 30 minutes–4 hours
away by fast ferry. Many travelers combine it with Coron for a northern Palawan trip.
